title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Introduction
content: The superior cervical ganglia are involved in the autonomic nervous system. They are involved explicitly with sympathetic efferent innervation, particularly to the face and head (see Figure. Sympathetic Nerves). The superior cervical ganglion is the most superior ganglion of the sympathetic chain, bilaterally. It is the largest of the 3 ganglia of the cervical sympathetic trunk, the other 2 being the stellate and middle cervical ganglia. [1] The superior cervical ganglia are approximately at the levels of the second cervical vertebra (C2) and the third cervical vertebra (C3), bilaterally. They typically lie bilaterally lateral to the longus colli muscles. The superior cervical ganglia usually lie anteromedially or medially to their respective internal carotid arteries. [1] [2] They are considered landmarks of the sympathetic trunk and typically provide sympathetic innervation to the head and neck. [3] [4] See Figure. Sympathetic Nerves, Connections Between the Submaxillary and Superior Cervical Ganglia.

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Structure and Function
content: The superior cervical ganglia are made up of the paravertebral ganglia of cervical vertebral levels 1 through 4 (C1-C4). [3] [4] The superior cervical ganglia are oval-shaped, cylinder-like, and elongated. They contain neurons. [1] [5] [6] They receive presynaptic signals from the sympathetic trunk. Postsynaptic signals then convey information from the superior cervical ganglia to targets in the head and neck. [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Embryology
content: The superior cervical ganglia derive from neural crest cells. Neural crest cells originate from the ectoderm during embryonic development. Many structures of the head, neck, face, and cardiovascular system also originate from the neural crest cells. [5] [7]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Branches from the ascending pharyngeal artery, coming off the external carotid artery, provide blood supply to the superior cervical ganglia. Venous drainage is through the internal jugular vein through direct posterior branches. There is a noted deficiency in gross blood supply at the junction of the upper one-third and lower two-thirds of the neck; this is important for surgical considerations mentioned in the latter part of this activity. [8] The superior cervical ganglia are anterior to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes. [1] [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Nerves
content: As previously described, the superior cervical ganglia are made up of the paravertebral ganglia of cervical vertebral levels 1 through 4 (C1-C4). [3] [4] The superior cervical ganglia themselves contain neurons that supply sympathetic innervation to the head and neck. [5] [6] The superior cervical ganglia provide postsynaptic fibers via the deep petrosal nerve to provide vasoconstriction to the lacrimal gland. [9] The superior cervical ganglia also supply gray rami communicantes to the ventral rami in the cervical plexus. [10] The superior cervical ganglia connect to the next closest ganglia, the middle cervical ganglia, inferiorly via the sympathetic trunk. [4]

content: The superior cervical ganglia provide sympathetic innervation.[10] Their location is lateral to the longus colli muscles. [1] [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Physiologic Variants
content: The superior cervical ganglia are typically present at cervical vertebral levels 1 and 2 (C1 and C2). However, they have been found between the cervical vertebral levels 1 through 5. (C1-C5). [1] The range of the length of the superior cervical ganglia is from 10 to 30mm. The width of the superior cervical ganglia ranges from 5 to 8mm. [1] See Figures. Cervical Portion of the Sympathetic System, Cervical Portion, Sympathetic System. Branches coming off the superior cervical ganglia include the: Pharyngeal branch The communicating branch of the cervical nerve The internal carotid branch The communicating branch of the pharyngeal mucosa The communicating branch of the vagus nerve The communicating branch of the superior laryngeal nerve The laryngeal branch The communicating branch of the internal jugular vein

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Physiologic Variants
content: There are reports of up to 7 different types of branch combinations coming off the superior cervical ganglia. [2] It is crucial to recognize that these are common variants of branches arising from the superior cervical ganglia, as damaging them may lead to Horner syndrome, as described later in this activity. [1]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Surgical Considerations
content: It is important to avoid injury to the superior cervical ganglia during open anterior neck surgeries. When the superior cervical ganglia are damaged, Horner syndrome can develop. Horner syndrome results from compression of the sympathetic trunk during anterior neck surgeries such as anterior cervical disc fusions. The tension damages the fibers along the sympathetic trunk. More about Horner syndrome is described later in this activity. [1] [4] [11] Knowing the anatomy and landmarks regarding the neck helps to avoid damaging important neurovasculature in the area. [1]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Surgical Considerations
content: Anterior surgical procedures in the neck, such as anterior cervical discectomies, can disrupt the blood supply to the superior cervical ganglia, leading to ischemic injury. This ischemic damage can also cause symptoms similar to Horner syndrome. [7] To prevent damage to the sympathetic ganglia during an anterior approach to the cervical spine, it is always advisable to create a longus colli gutter and then place the retractors within the same, thereby minimizing the risk of inadvertent injury to the ganglia that lie lateral to the muscle.

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Clinical Significance
content: The superior cervical ganglia can be a site for locally injected anesthetics such as opioids, which is useful for neuropathic pain management of the face. [1] [2] The superior cervical ganglia are the main source of sympathetic innervation to the head and face. Buprenorphine has been specifically utilized in these ganglionic local opioid analgesia injections to provide pain relief to patients suffering from neuropathic facial pain stemming from atypical facial pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and trigeminal neuralgia. [12] Understanding the anatomic positioning of the superior cervical ganglia allows this injection to be performed safely by avoiding important structures, such as the internal carotid arteries, which lie close to them. [1] [2] [12] Ultrasound guidance can be utilized to visualize the superior cervical ganglia properly during this procedure. [12]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Clinical Significance
content: Damage to the superior cervical ganglia can cause a postganglionic pattern of Horner syndrome. The symptoms of Horner syndrome include miosis, facial anhidrosis, and partial ptosis; this is due to the superior cervical ganglia's role in providing sympathetic innervation to these targets. [4] [11] These symptoms arise from disruption of the sympathetic nervous system, including the superior cervical ganglia. Care is necessary during superior cervical ganglion blocks and head and neck procedures to prevent Horner syndrome. [11]

title: Neuroanatomy, Superior Cervical Ganglion -- Other Issues
content: The superior cervical ganglion can appear as pathologic retropharyngeal lymph nodes on imaging. The superior cervical ganglia are anterior to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes. [1] [2] The proximity of the superior cervical ganglia to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes can make the staging of neck neoplasms difficult. Nasopharyngeal cancer, thyroid cancer, and oropharyngeal cancer typically metastasize to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes; delineating them from the superior cervical ganglia is very important. [1] [2] [3] Magnetic resonance imaging can be used to distinguish pathologic retropharyngeal lymph nodes from the superior ganglia. [1] [2]
